The Spouter-Inn, a gable-ended old house, is the setting for Ishmael's first night in New Bedford. The inn's entrance is a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned wainscots. Ishmael finds an oil painting on the wall, which is "thoroughly besmoked and every way defaced." Despite its condition, the painting depicts a Cape-Horner in a great hurricane, with an exasperated whale about to spring clean over the craft. The painting's meaning is unclear, but Ishmael is drawn to it.

The interior of the inn is dimly lit, and Ishmael notices a heathenish array of monstrous clubs and spears on the wall. These clubs and spears are decorated with human hair, teeth, and other gruesome features. Ishmael also sees old whaling lances and harpoons, some of which are broken and deformed.

Ishmael approaches the landlord and asks to be accommodated with a room. The landlord tells him that his house is full, but Ishmael can share a harpooneer's blanket. Ishmael agrees, but is skeptical about the harpooneer. The landlord warns Ishmael that the harpooneer is a bit of an eccentric, but Ishmael is undeterred.

Ishmael sits down on an old wooden settle and observes the other boarders. They are a rough-looking bunch, but Ishmael is fascinated by their stories and experiences. He asks the landlord about the harpooneer, and the landlord tells him that the harpooneer is a bit of a mystery. Ishmael decides to wait and see if the harpooneer will show up before deciding whether to share a bed with him.

As Ishmael waits, he reflects on his decision to sail to sea and how it brings him a sense of relief and escape from his troubles. He believes that the sea has a mystical power that draws people to it, and that it is a place of freedom and adventure.

The harpooneer, Queequeg, arrives, and Ishmael is surprised by his exotic appearance and customs. Queequeg is a skilled harpooneer from a remote island and is a member of a pagan tribe. Ishmael is initially hesitant to share a bed with Queequeg, but eventually warms up to him.

Ishmael learns about Queequeg's island and his desire to learn among Christians. Queequeg has been disillusioned by the practices of whalemen and has given up on the idea of becoming a Christian. Ishmael is fascinated by Queequeg's story and begins to see him as a kindred spirit.

The two men share a bed and begin to form a bond. Ishmael is drawn to Queequeg's pagan ways and begins to see the beauty in them. He also learns about Queequeg's idol, Yojo, which is a small wooden figure that Queequeg treats with great respect.

As the night wears on, Ishmael and Queequeg engage in conversation and share stories. Ishmael is fascinated by Queequeg's island and his people. Queequeg tells Ishmael about his desire to visit Christendom and learn among Christians. Ishmael is intrigued by Queequeg's story and begins to see him as a kindred spirit.

The two men eventually fall asleep, but Ishmael is woken up by the sound of Queequeg's snores. Ishmael reflects on the strange and unfamiliar customs of the whaling world and the men who inhabit it.

The next morning, Ishmael and Queequeg set off for Nantucket, where they will join a whaling ship. Ishmael is excited to embark on his adventure and see the world. Queequeg is also eager to join the whaling ship and continue his quest for knowledge and adventure.

Upon arriving in Nantucket, Ishmael and Queequeg visit the Try Pots, a hotel run by Mrs. Hussey, who serves them a delicious clam chowder. Ishmael is impressed by the hotel's reputation for serving excellent chowder and is eager to try it. Queequeg is equally enthusiastic, as clams are a favorite food of his.

As they enjoy their meal, Ishmael reflects on the unique culture and traditions of Nantucket. He notes that the island's residents are a mix of old and new, with a blend of traditional and modern influences. Ishmael is struck by the island's beauty and the sense of community that pervades it.

After finishing their meal, Ishmael and Queequeg set off to find a ship to join. They visit the Pequod, a whaling ship that is preparing to set sail. Ishmael is drawn to the ship's history and the stories of its crew. He is particularly interested in the ship's captain, Ahab, who is known for his fierce determination and obsession with hunting the white whale, Moby Dick.

As Ishmael and Queequeg explore the ship, they meet Elijah, a strange and eccentric sailor who seems to be obsessed with Captain Ahab. Elijah warns Ishmael and Queequeg to be careful around Ahab, but Ishmael is not sure what to make of him.

The narrator, Ishmael, recounts his experiences on the whaleship Pequod, captained by Ahab. Ahab's obsession with hunting the white whale Moby Dick has consumed him, and he is determined to pursue the whale to the ends of the earth. The crew is gathered on the quarterdeck, and Ahab announces that he will give a reward to anyone who can bring him the white whale, describing its unique characteristics, including its white color, wrinkled brow, and crooked jaw.

The crew is enthusiastic and begins to chant and shout, but Starbuck, the first mate, is skeptical and asks if Ahab's vendetta will bring them any profit. Ahab responds by explaining that his revenge is not about money, but about the principle of the thing. He sees the white whale as a manifestation of the unknowable and unreasoning forces of nature, and he believes that by striking at the whale, he is striking at the mask that hides the true nature of the universe.

The crew is undeterred by Ahab's words and agrees to join him in his quest. Ahab then orders the crew to produce their harpoons, and the three harpooneers, Queequeg, Tashtego, and Daggoo, stand at attention with their harpoons. Ahab fills the harpoon sockets with liquor and orders the crew to drink and swear their allegiance to the hunt.

As the sun sets, Ahab sits alone in his cabin, lost in thought. He reflects on his past and the prophecy that he will be dismembered, which has come true in the loss of his leg. He now prophesies that he will dismember his dismemberer, Moby Dick. Ahab feels a sense of inevitability and certainty in his actions, as if he is driven by a force beyond his control.

Meanwhile, Starbuck leans against the mainmast, struggling with his own doubts and fears. He sees Ahab as a madman who has lost his reason and is now driven by a demonic force. Starbuck feels a sense of pity and obligation towards Ahab, but also a sense of rebellion and resentment. He knows that he must obey Ahab, but he hates the old man with a touch of pity.

The crew's revelry in the forecastle is in stark contrast to the somber and oppressive atmosphere on the quarterdeck. The narrator describes the scene as a picture of life, with the bow of the ship shooting forward into the sparkling sea, while Ahab broods in his cabin, surrounded by the dead water of the wake.
